1	# TIOBE Programming Community Index -- March 2026 Monthly Report
2	
3	## Source
4	
5	- URL: https://www.tiobe.com/tiobe-index/
6	- Captured: April 10, 2026
7	- Author: Paul Jansen, CEO, TIOBE Software
8	
9	The TIOBE Programming Community Index is a widely cited indicator of programming language popularity, updated monthly since 2001. Ratings are calculated from the number of skilled engineers worldwide, training courses, and third-party vendors, using search-engine hit counts across Google, Amazon, Wikipedia, Bing, and more than 20 other sites. The index does not measure which language is "best" or which has the most lines of code written; rather, it reflects how much a language is discussed and sought after on the public internet.
10	
11	## March 2026 Headline: Why the TIOBE Index Still Relies on Search Engines
12	
13	The March 2026 editorial addresses a recurring question: should the TIOBE index switch from search-engine hit counts to LLM-based assessments of language popularity? Paul Jansen explains that the answer is no. LLMs are ultimately trained on the same web pages that search engines index, so querying an LLM would not yield fundamentally different data. The methodology therefore remains anchored to direct measurement of web-page volume per language.
14	
15	Beyond the methodology discussion, the March update records several notable rank changes. SQL and R swapped positions within the top 10, with R climbing from 16th to 9th year-over-year. Swift re-entered the top 20 at the expense of Kotlin, and Ruby is on the verge of dropping out of the top 30.
16	
17	## Top 20 Programming Languages -- March 2026
18	
19	![Top 20 programming languages ranked by TIOBE rating, March 2026](./assets/table_top20_rankings.jpg)
20	
21	| Rank (Mar 2026) | Rank (Mar 2025) | Programming Language | Rating | YoY Change |
22	|:---:|:---:|------|:---:|:---:|
23	| 1 | 1 | Python | 21.25% | -2.59% |
24	| 2 | 4 | C | 11.55% | +2.02% |
25	| 3 | 2 | C++ | 8.18% | -2.90% |
26	| 4 | 3 | Java | 7.99% | -2.37% |
27	| 5 | 5 | C# | 6.36% | +1.49% |
28	| 6 | 6 | JavaScript | 3.45% | -0.01% |
29	| 7 | 9 | Visual Basic | 2.50% | -0.02% |
30	| 8 | 8 | SQL | 2.00% | -0.57% |
31	| 9 | 16 | R | 1.88% | +0.94% |
32	| 10 | 10 | Delphi/Object Pascal | 1.80% | -0.36% |
33	| 11 | 24 | Perl | 1.75% | +1.05% |
34	| 12 | 12 | Scratch | 1.63% | -0.03% |
35	| 13 | 11 | Fortran | 1.45% | -0.25% |
36	| 14 | 14 | Rust | 1.31% | +0.09% |
37	| 15 | 15 | MATLAB | 1.29% | +0.31% |
38	| 16 | 7 | Go | 1.29% | -1.49% |
39	| 17 | 17 | Assembly language | 1.29% | +0.42% |
40	| 18 | 13 | PHP | 1.23% | -0.25% |
41	| 19 | 18 | Ada | 1.10% | +0.25% |
42	| 20 | 26 | Swift | 1.04% | +0.44% |
43	
44	Python holds the top position at 21.25%, more than double the rating of second-place C (11.55%). However, Python's year-over-year change is -2.59 percentage points, while C gained +2.02 points. The top 4 languages -- Python, C, C++, and Java -- collectively account for nearly 49% of the total index.
45	
46	## Historical Trend: Two Decades of Language Popularity (2002--2026)
47	
48	![Historical popularity trends for the top 10 programming languages from 2002 to 2026](./assets/chart_historical_trends.jpg)
49	
50	The TIOBE index publishes a long-running trend chart covering the top 10 languages from 2002 to the present. Key patterns visible in the data:
51	
52	- **Python's meteoric rise**: From a minor language ranked around 8th in 2006, Python surged to the top position after 2018, peaking above 25% before settling at 21.25% in March 2026.
53	- **C's resilience**: C has held a top-2 position for most of the 24-year span, with periodic surges (notably around 2015 and again in 2025--2026).
54	- **Java's long decline**: Java dominated the index from roughly 2005 to 2018, but has steadily fallen from the 25%+ range to under 8%.
55	- **JavaScript's plateau**: Despite its dominance in web development, JavaScript has never exceeded roughly 5% on the TIOBE index and currently sits at 3.45%.
56	
57	## Very Long Term History: Rank Positions Across Four Decades
58	
59	![Long-term ranking history of selected programming languages from 1986 to 2026](./assets/table_long_term_history.jpg)
60	
61	| Language | 2026 | 2021 | 2016 | 2011 | 2006 | 2001 | 1996 | 1991 | 1986 |
62	|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
63	| Python | 1 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 8 | 26 | 17 | - | - |
64	| C | 2 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
65	| C++ | 3 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 9 |
66	| Java | 4 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 3 | 31 | - | - |
67	| C# | 5 | 5 | 4 | 5 | 7 | 11 | - | - | - |
68	| JavaScript | 6 | 7 | 8 | 10 | 10 | 8 | 33 | - | - |
69	| Go | 10 | 11 | 60 | 16 | - | - | - | - | - |
70	| Ada | 14 | 36 | 25 | 22 | 16 | 18 | 6 | 10 | 3 |
71	| Lisp | 26 | 34 | 26 | 13 | 14 | 19 | 8 | 4 | 2 |
72	
73	This table reveals dramatic shifts across decades. Python was unranked before 1991, entered the top 30 only by 2001, and took 25 years to reach the top position. Conversely, Lisp was the number-2 language in 1986 but has fallen to 26th. Ada peaked at 3rd in 1986 and now sits at 14th. C is the only language that has remained in the top 2 across all nine measurement points.
74	
75	## Programming Language Hall of Fame
76	
77	![Hall of Fame -- Language of the Year winners from 2003 to 2025](./assets/table_hall_of_fame.jpg)
78	
79	The TIOBE "Programming Language of the Year" award goes to the language with the largest gain in ratings during a calendar year. Recent winners include:
80	
81	| Year | Winner |
82	|:---:|------|
83	| 2025 | C# |
84	| 2024 | Python |
85	| 2023 | C# |
86	| 2022 | C++ |
87	| 2021 | Python |
88	| 2020 | Python |
89	| 2019 | C |
90	| 2018 | Python |
91	| 2016 | Go |
92	
93	Python has won the award five times (2007, 2010, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2024), more than any other language. C# took the title in both 2023 and 2025, reflecting its continued growth driven by the .NET ecosystem.
94	
95	## Key Findings
96	
97	- **Python remains dominant but is losing ground**: At 21.25%, Python leads by a wide margin, yet its year-over-year decline of -2.59 percentage points is the largest drop among the top 5. C, by contrast, gained +2.02 points and climbed from 4th to 2nd.
98	- **Legacy languages show surprising resilience**: Perl jumped from 24th to 11th (+1.05%), R rose from 16th to 9th (+0.94%), and Fortran remains in the top 15. These languages continue to serve entrenched communities in scientific computing, data analysis, and infrastructure.
99	- **Go suffers its sharpest decline**: Go fell from 7th to 16th, losing 1.49 percentage points -- the largest absolute drop of any top-20 language. This contrasts with its 2016 "Language of the Year" win and suggests possible displacement by Rust (14th, +0.09%) in the systems programming space.
100	- **Swift re-enters the top 20, Kotlin exits**: Swift climbed from 26th to 20th (+0.44%), while Kotlin dropped to 22nd. In the mobile development ecosystem, Swift's gains may reflect Apple platform growth, while Kotlin faces competition from cross-platform frameworks.
101	- **The top 4 languages hold nearly half the index**: Python, C, C++, and Java together account for 48.97% of total TIOBE ratings, illustrating how concentrated the programming landscape remains despite 50+ tracked languages.
102

# TIOBE Programming Community Index -- March 2026 Monthly Report

## Source

- URL: https://www.tiobe.com/tiobe-index/
- Captured: April 10, 2026
- Author: Paul Jansen, CEO, TIOBE Software

The TIOBE Programming Community Index is a widely cited indicator of programming language popularity, updated monthly since 2001. Ratings are calculated from the number of skilled engineers worldwide, training courses, and third-party vendors, using search-engine hit counts across Google, Amazon, Wikipedia, Bing, and more than 20 other sites. The index does not measure which language is "best" or which has the most lines of code written; rather, it reflects how much a language is discussed and sought after on the public internet.

## March 2026 Headline: Why the TIOBE Index Still Relies on Search Engines

The March 2026 editorial addresses a recurring question: should the TIOBE index switch from search-engine hit counts to LLM-based assessments of language popularity? Paul Jansen explains that the answer is no. LLMs are ultimately trained on the same web pages that search engines index, so querying an LLM would not yield fundamentally different data. The methodology therefore remains anchored to direct measurement of web-page volume per language.

Beyond the methodology discussion, the March update records several notable rank changes. SQL and R swapped positions within the top 10, with R climbing from 16th to 9th year-over-year. Swift re-entered the top 20 at the expense of Kotlin, and Ruby is on the verge of dropping out of the top 30.

## Top 20 Programming Languages -- March 2026

| 2021 | Python |

LOSS_RED   = RGBColor(0xF4, 0x5B, 0x69)   # red for losers

def new_prs():

    prs.slide_width  = SLIDE_W
    prs.slide_height = SLIDE_H
    return prs


def blank_slide(prs):
    layout = prs.slide_layouts[6]  # blank
    return prs.slides.add_slide(layout)


def fill_bg(slide, color):
    background = slide.background
    fill = background.fill
    fill.solid()
    fill.fore_color.rgb = color


def add_rect(slide, l, t, w, h, fill_color=None, line_color=None, line_width=Pt(0)):
    from pptx.util import Pt
    shape = slide.shapes.add_shape(1, l, t, w, h)  # MSO_SHAPE_TYPE.RECTANGLE = 1
    shape.line.width = line_width
    if fill_color:
        shape.fill.solid()
        shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = fill_color
    else:
        shape.fill.background()
    if line_color:
        shape.line.color.rgb = line_color
    else:
        shape.line.fill.background()
    return shape


def add_text_box(slide, text, l, t, w, h, font_size=Pt(14), bold=False,
                 color=WHITE, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, wrap=True, italic=False):
    txBox = slide.shapes.add_textbox(l, t, w, h)
    tf = txBox.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = wrap
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.alignment = align
    run = p.add_run()
    run.text = text
    run.font.size = font_size
    run.font.bold = bold
    run.font.italic = italic
    run.font.color.rgb = color
    return txBox

def fill_bg(slide, color):
    background = slide.background
    fill = background.fill
    fill.solid()
    fill.fore_color.rgb = color


def add_rect(slide, l, t, w, h, fill_color=None, line_color=None, line_width=Pt(0)):
    from pptx.util import Pt
    shape = slide.shapes.add_shape(1, l, t, w, h)  # MSO_SHAPE_TYPE.RECTANGLE = 1
    shape.line.width = line_width
    if fill_color:
        shape.fill.solid()
        shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = fill_color
    else:
        shape.fill.background()
    if line_color:
        shape.line.color.rgb = line_color
    else:
        shape.line.fill.background()
    return shape


def add_text_box(slide, text, l, t, w, h, font_size=Pt(14), bold=False,
                 color=WHITE, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, wrap=True, italic=False):
    txBox = slide.shapes.add_textbox(l, t, w, h)
    tf = txBox.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = wrap
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.alignment = align
    run = p.add_run()
    run.text = text
    run.font.size = font_size
    run.font.bold = bold
    run.font.italic = italic
    run.font.color.rgb = color
    return txBox

        add_rect(sl, bar_x, ry, bar_w, bar_h, fill_color=GAIN_GRN)
        # language label left of bar
        add_text_box(sl, lang, Inches(0.25), ry, Inches(1.5), bar_h,
                     font_size=Pt(11), bold=True, color=WHITE, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
        # rank change bubble
        add_rect(sl, Inches(4.4), ry, Inches(1.1), bar_h, fill_color=BG_CARD, line_color=GAIN_GRN, line_width=Pt(1))
        add_text_box(sl, label, Inches(4.4), ry, Inches(1.1), bar_h,
                     font_size=Pt(9), bold=True, color=GAIN_GRN, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)
        add_text_box(sl, pct, Inches(5.55), ry, Inches(0.9), bar_h,
                     font_size=Pt(9), color=GAIN_GRN, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

    # Losers (bars growing rightward from centre line)
    loser_max = 9
    for i, (lang, prev, cur, pct, label) in enumerate(losers):
        ry = row_top + i * row_gap
        spots = cur - prev
        bar_w = bar_max_w * (spots / loser_max)
        bar_x = Inches(7.2)

        add_rect(sl, bar_x, ry, bar_w, bar_h, fill_color=LOSS_RED)
        add_text_box(sl, lang, Inches(7.2), ry, Inches(1.5), bar_h,
                     font_size=Pt(11), bold=True, color=WHITE, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
        add_rect(sl, Inches(8.65), ry, Inches(1.1), bar_h, fill_color=BG_CARD, line_color=LOSS_RED, line_width=Pt(1))
        add_text_box(sl, label, Inches(8.65), ry, Inches(1.1), bar_h,
                     font_size=Pt(9), bold=True, color=LOSS_RED, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)
        add_text_box(sl, pct, Inches(9.8), ry, Inches(0.9), bar_h,
                     font_size=Pt(9), color=LOSS_RED, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

    # Insight note
    add_rect(sl, Inches(0.25), SLIDE_H - Inches(0.95), SLIDE_W - Inches(0.5), Inches(0.6),
             fill_color=BG_CARD, line_color=ACCENT2, line_width=Pt(0.75))
    add_text_box(sl,
        "Key insight: Go's -9-spot collapse suggests displacement by Rust in systems programming, "
        "while Perl & R demonstrate that legacy languages serving entrenched scientific communities remain resilient.",
        Inches(0.4), SLIDE_H - Inches(0.93), SLIDE_W - Inches(0.8), Inches(0.56),
        font_size=Pt(10), color=ACCENT2, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

    return sl


# ── SLIDE 4 : Historical ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LONG_TERM = [
    ("Python",     [1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 26, 17, "-", "-"]),
    ("C",          [2, 1, 2, 2, 2,  1,  1,  1,   1]),
    ("C++",        [3, 4, 3, 3, 3,  2,  2,  2,   9]),
    ("Java",       [4, 2, 1, 1, 1,  3, 31,  "-", "-"]),
    ("C#",         [5, 5, 4, 5, 7, 11,  "-", "-", "-"]),
    ("JavaScript", [6, 7, 8,10,10,  8, 33,  "-", "-"]),
    ("Go",         [10,11,60,16,"-","-","-", "-", "-"]),
    ("Ada",        [14,36,25,22,16, 18,  6,  10,   3]),
    ("Lisp",       [26,34,26,13,14, 19,  8,   4,   2]),
]
YEARS = ["2026","2021","2016","2011","2006","2001","1996","1991","1986"]

def slide_historical(prs):
    sl = blank_slide(prs)
    fill_bg(sl, BG_DARK)
    slide_header(sl,
        "From Lisp at #2 in 1986 to Python at #1 in 2026: How Language Rankings Shifted Over Time",
        subtitle="Rank snapshots every 5 years across four decades · 2002–2026 trend summary")

    t_top = Inches(1.52)
    row_h = Inches(0.38)
    col0_w = Inches(1.55)
    yr_w   = Inches(1.05)
    table_l = Inches(0.3)

    # Header row
    add_rect(sl, table_l, t_top, Inches(12.7), row_h, fill_color=ACCENT)
    add_text_box(sl, "Language", table_l + Inches(0.05), t_top, col0_w, row_h,
                 font_size=Pt(9), bold=True, color=BG_DARK, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
    for yi, yr in enumerate(YEARS):
        add_text_box(sl, yr, table_l + col0_w + yi * yr_w, t_top, yr_w, row_h,
                     font_size=Pt(9), bold=True, color=BG_DARK, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

    highlight_cells = {
        ("Python", "2026"), ("C", "2026"), ("C", "1986"), ("C", "1991"),
        ("C", "1996"), ("C", "2001"), ("Python", "1986"),
    }
    for ri, (lang, ranks) in enumerate(LONG_TERM):
        ry = t_top + row_h * (ri + 1)
        row_bg = BG_CARD if ri % 2 == 0 else BG_DARK
        add_rect(sl, table_l, ry, Inches(12.7), row_h, fill_color=row_bg)
        lang_col = ACCENT if lang in ("Python", "C") else WHITE
        add_text_box(sl, lang, table_l + Inches(0.05), ry, col0_w, row_h,
                     font_size=Pt(9), bold=(lang in ("Python","C")), color=lang_col, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
        for yi, (yr, rank) in enumerate(zip(YEARS, ranks)):
            cell_x = table_l + col0_w + yi * yr_w
            rank_str = str(rank)
            if rank_str == "-":
                txt_col = MID_GRAY
            elif isinstance(rank, int) and rank <= 3:
                txt_col = ACCENT2
            elif (lang, yr) in highlight_cells:
                txt_col = ACCENT
            else:
                txt_col = LIGHT_GRAY
            add_text_box(sl, rank_str, cell_x, ry, yr_w, row_h,
                         font_size=Pt(9), bold=(isinstance(rank,int) and rank<=2),
                         color=txt_col, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

    # Trend summary bullets
    bullet_top = t_top + row_h * 10 + Inches(0.1)
    bullets = [
        ("Python", GAIN_GRN,
         "Unranked in 1986 → #1 in 2026. Surpassed Java post-2018, peaked >25%, now at 21.25%."),
        ("C",      ACCENT,
         "Only language ranked #1 or #2 across all nine measurement points spanning 40 years."),
        ("Java",   LOSS_RED,
         "Dominated 2005–2018 at 25%+. Steady decline to 7.99% — still #4, but a long fall."),
        ("Lisp",   MID_GRAY,
         "#2 in 1986, now #26. A cautionary tale: ecosystem stagnation erodes community mindshare."),
    ]
    bw = Inches(3.0)
    bh = Inches(0.72)
    for i, (tag, col, txt) in enumerate(bullets):
        bx = Inches(0.3) + i * Inches(3.26)
        by = bullet_top
        add_rect(sl, bx, by, bw, bh, fill_color=BG_CARD, line_color=col, line_width=Pt(1))
        add_text_box(sl, tag, bx + Inches(0.1), by + Inches(0.02), bw - Inches(0.2), Inches(0.22),
                     font_size=Pt(9), bold=True, color=col, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
        add_text_box(sl, txt, bx + Inches(0.1), by + Inches(0.22), bw - Inches(0.2), Inches(0.48),
                     font_size=Pt(8), color=LIGHT_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

    return sl


# ── SLIDE 5 : Hall of Fame ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

HOF = [
    (2025, "C#",     GAIN_GRN),
    (2024, "Python", GAIN_GRN),
    (2023, "C#",     GAIN_GRN),
    (2022, "C++",    LIGHT_GRAY),
    (2021, "Python", GAIN_GRN),
    (2020, "Python", GAIN_GRN),
    (2019, "C",      LIGHT_GRAY),
    (2018, "Python", GAIN_GRN),
    (2016, "Go",     LOSS_RED),
]

def slide_hof(prs):
    sl = blank_slide(prs)
    fill_bg(sl, BG_DARK)
    slide_header(sl,
        "Python Wins Language of the Year 6 Times — More Than Any Other Language",
        subtitle="TIOBE 'Language of the Year' — largest rating gain in that calendar year")

    body_top = Inches(1.52)

    # Trophy visual: timeline of cards
    card_w = Inches(1.28)
    card_h = Inches(1.6)
    card_gap = Inches(0.18)
    total_w = len(HOF) * card_w + (len(HOF)-1) * card_gap
    start_x = (SLIDE_W - total_w) / 2

    for i, (year, lang, col) in enumerate(HOF):
        cx = start_x + i * (card_w + card_gap)
        cy = body_top
        # card
        add_rect(sl, cx, cy, card_w, card_h, fill_color=BG_CARD,
                 line_color=col, line_width=Pt(1.5))
        # year
        add_text_box(sl, str(year), cx, cy + Inches(0.08), card_w, Inches(0.32),
                     font_size=Pt(12), bold=True, color=MID_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)
        # trophy emoji substitute — star
        add_rect(sl, cx + Inches(0.44), cy + Inches(0.42), Inches(0.4), Inches(0.4),
                 fill_color=col)
        # language name
        add_text_box(sl, lang, cx, cy + Inches(0.92), card_w, Inches(0.5),
                     font_size=Pt(13), bold=True, color=col, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)
        # note for notable
        if lang == "Go":
            add_text_box(sl, "Now #16", cx, cy + Inches(1.38), card_w, Inches(0.2),
                         font_size=Pt(7.5), color=LOSS_RED, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

    # Note about 2017
    add_text_box(sl, "Note: 2017 winner not available in source data.",
                 Inches(0.4), body_top + card_h + Inches(0.08),
                 Inches(8), Inches(0.25),
                 font_size=Pt(9), color=MID_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, italic=True)

    # Stat panels
    stats_top = body_top + card_h + Inches(0.45)
    stats = [
        ("6×", "Python wins\n(most of any language)", GAIN_GRN),
        ("2×", "C# wins in 2023 & 2025\n(.NET ecosystem growth)", ACCENT),
        ("2016", "Go's only win —\nnow its biggest irony", LOSS_RED),
        ("2022", "C++ resurged before\nits current -2.90% slide", ACCENT2),
    ]
    sw = Inches(3.0)
    sh = Inches(1.35)
    sg = Inches(0.44)
    sx0 = Inches(0.4)
    for i, (stat, label, col) in enumerate(stats):
        sx = sx0 + i * (sw + sg)
        add_rect(sl, sx, stats_top, sw, sh, fill_color=BG_CARD, line_color=col, line_width=Pt(1))
        add_text_box(sl, stat, sx, stats_top + Inches(0.1), sw, Inches(0.55),
                     font_size=Pt(32), bold=True, color=col, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)
        add_text_box(sl, label, sx + Inches(0.1), stats_top + Inches(0.65), sw - Inches(0.2), Inches(0.65),
                     font_size=Pt(9.5), color=LIGHT_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

    return sl


# ── SLIDE 6 : Takeaways ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def slide_takeaways(prs):
    sl = blank_slide(prs)
    fill_bg(sl, BG_DARK)
    slide_header(sl,
        "The Top 4 Languages Hold 49% of the Index: What This Means for Your Tech Stack",
        subtitle="Actionable implications for hiring, training, and tooling decisions")

    body_top = Inches(1.52)

    # Five takeaway cards in a 3+2 layout
    cards = [
        ("Python Dominates but Declines",
         LOSS_RED,
         "At 21.25%, Python leads by 2×. Yet its -2.59 pp YoY drop is the largest among top-5. "
         "Maintain Python investment — but monitor the trend. Evaluate whether C's surge signals a "
         "shift back to low-level systems work in your stack."),

        ("C's Resurgence Is Real",
         ACCENT,
         "C jumped from #4 to #2 with +2.02 pp — the top gainer. Combined with Rust at #14 (+0.09%), "
         "systems-level programming is regaining mindshare. Embedded, OS, and performance-critical "
         "teams should plan for increased C/Rust talent demand."),

        ("Legacy Languages Aren't Dead",
         ACCENT2,
         "Perl (+13 spots), R (+7 spots), and Fortran (still top-15) defy write-offs. "
         "Scientific computing, genomics, and data-pipeline teams still run on these. "
         "Avoid abrupt re-platforming without assessing the real cost to entrenched communities."),

        ("Go's 9-Spot Drop Is a Warning",
         LOSS_RED,
         "Go fell from #7 to #16 in one year — the steepest decline in the top 20. "
         "If Go is central to your microservices strategy, assess whether Rust or other "
         "alternatives are drawing community energy away. Watch TIOBE over the next 2 quarters."),

        ("Concentration Risk: 49% in 4 Languages",
         GAIN_GRN,
         "Python + C + C++ + Java = 48.97% of all TIOBE ratings. Betting your hiring pipeline on "
         "only these four is efficient today but fragile long-term. Build polyglot capability. "
         "C# (6.36%, 2× Language of the Year) and Rust (1.31%, rising) are credible next bets."),
    ]

    cw3 = Inches(4.1)
    cw2 = Inches(6.2)
    ch  = Inches(1.9)
    ct1 = body_top
    ct2 = body_top + ch + Inches(0.18)
    gap = Inches(0.22)

    positions = [
        (Inches(0.28), ct1, cw3),
        (Inches(0.28) + cw3 + gap, ct1, cw3),
        (Inches(0.28) + 2*(cw3 + gap), ct1, cw3),
        (Inches(0.28), ct2, cw2),
        (Inches(0.28) + cw2 + gap, ct2, cw2),
    ]

    for (cx, cy, cw), (title, col, body) in zip(positions, cards):
        add_rect(sl, cx, cy, cw, ch, fill_color=BG_CARD, line_color=col, line_width=Pt(1.5))
        # colour bar top of card
        add_rect(sl, cx, cy, cw, Inches(0.06), fill_color=col)
        add_text_box(sl, title, cx + Inches(0.1), cy + Inches(0.1), cw - Inches(0.2), Inches(0.32),
                     font_size=Pt(10), bold=True, color=col, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)
        add_text_box(sl, body, cx + Inches(0.1), cy + Inches(0.42), cw - Inches(0.2), ch - Inches(0.5),
                     font_size=Pt(8.5), color=LIGHT_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

    return sl


# ── BUILD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

prs = new_prs()
slide_title(prs)
slide_top20(prs)
slide_movers(prs)
slide_historical(prs)
slide_hof(prs)
slide_takeaways(prs)

out = "/app/output/final_deck.pptx"
prs.save(out)
print(f"Saved → {out}")
